paper_title: ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

To bridge this gap, we introduce Physical-Time Flow (PT-Flow), novel approach that learns continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in well-structured dynamical representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of the future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct ODEWorld, continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction with ODEWorld even after long-horizon prediction. Comprehensive experiments across multiple simulation and real-world datasets demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: The physical world we inhabit is fundamentally continuous in both space and time. In our daily life, objects move, interact, and collide in continuous time, governed entirely by underlying physical laws; meanwhile, biological organisms, such as humans and animals, are naturally attuned to the perception, understanding, and decision-making of continuous transitions. Despite this, contemporary AI models almost exclusively rely on discrete-time modeling paradigms, such as modeling video as sequences of image frames (Ho et al., 2022; Bruce et al., 2024; Brooks et al., 2024; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b) and solving decision-making tasks in discrete time steps (Kim et al., 2026; Sutton et al., 1998; Hansen et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). This inherent discrepancy makes modern predictive architectures highly inflexible when handling irregularly sampled data, imposing strict requirements on data for temporal alignment during both training and generation (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2023). Furthermore, simply relying on learning discretetime pixel/sensor measurement transitions ignores the fundamental continuity in physics-grounded systems, causing current models to function primarily as video-mimicking, and become inefficient in internalizing the intrinsic, higher-order physics inherent in reality (Cellier and Greifeneder, 2013; Krishnapriyan et al., 2023). To bridge this gap, we introduce the concept of Physical-Time Flow (PT-Flow). At its core, PT-Flow conceptualizes the underlying dynamics in the data as continuous velocity field in well-structured latent space, where the latent state transition is smoothly governed by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) along 1 actual physical time. To make such continuous modeling framework possible, PT-Flow features two critical designs: 1) dynamical representation decoupling and 2) direct first-order supervision. The former decouples the time-varying, dynamics-related information from the data into clean, ODE-compatible dynamical representation space, getting rid of the nuanced background and time-invariant details for efficient learning. The latter directly supervises the latent velocity field with the approximated ground truth latent velocities through an elegant Jacobian-vector product (JVP) projection. The above two designs lead to new predictive architecture, in which the prediction of the future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space, in some sense similar to flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023), but operating in physical time. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct continuous-time latent world model, called ODEWorld, which embodies many desirable features. First, it disentangles dynamical representation by conditioning the encoder and decoder directly on static context, thereby offloading the burden of dynamical representation learning, allowing the latent space to focus exclusively on capturing essential dynamical changes. Second, ODEWorld circumvents the long-standing challenge of representation collapse in Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA)-based frameworks (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025), where the latent space can degenerate into trivial solutions due to the indirect supervision of the coupled encoder and latent predictor. While some recent efforts (Wang et al., 2026a; Maes et al., 2026) have added external regularization schemes to mitigate this issue, however, at the expense of sacrificing model expressiveness. By contrast, ODEWorld imposes direct supervision on the latent velocity field while harmoniously regularizing the ODE properties of the dynamical representations. These architectural choices empower ODEWorld to achieve high-fidelity image reconstruction with an extremely compact model, even across extended temporal horizons. Moreover, its continuous nature also enables arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward predictioncapabilities fundamentally absent in most discrete-time predictive models. Empirical evaluations across diverse simulation and real-world benchmark datasets, including LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and Agibot-World (Bu et al., 2025), demonstrate that ODEWorld effectively reconciles planningconducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism. We show that the learned latent velocity field produces interpretable and smooth transformation paths between the given initial and goal states. This well-behaved continuous latent flow enables temporally consistent, long-horizon predictions by leveraging off-the-shelf ODE solvers within highly compact latent manifold. Moreover, prediction by solving the continuous-time ODE naturally supports temporal super-resolution and robust video generation from irregularly sampled or dropped-frame data, where discrete-time models inherently fail. Lastly, robotic control experiments on the LIBERO Benchmark also reveal that ODEWorld extracts rich, planning-centric representations that can greatly facilitate downstream policy learning. Ultimately, these capabilities establish ODEWorld as highly versatile architecture, setting new continuous recipe for both high-fidelity video synthesis and effective robotic policy learning.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Predictive world models. Recent video generation models have achieved notable progress and shown great promise as scalable generative simulators of the physical world (Brooks et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Yang et al.; Bjorck et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2025). These models learn to predict future observations as surrogate for physical dynamics, producing full trajectory videos (Du et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024) or subgoal images (Black et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). These models also garnered substantial attention from the robotics community, which translates their video prediction capability to control. first line of methods adopts planning-and-control paradigm, where actions are inferred from predicted videos, via inverse dynamics models (Du et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024), goal-conditioned policies (Black et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Pai et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a), or direct pose extraction using off-the-shelf foundation models (Liang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025). second line of work instead integrates action generation into the world model, learning the joint distributions over future observations and actions (Li et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Cheang et al., 2024; Bi et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025). However, all of these models suffer from heavy architecture due to costly pixel-level reconstruction to derive world understanding, which have long been critiqued for their fundamental computational inefficiency. To address the efficiency issue, another branch of work focuses on learning latent world models, where 2 predictions are performed in compact representation space (Assran et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026). These approaches construct latent representations through various objectives, including image reconstruction (Hu et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025), contrastive learning (Liu et al., 2025; Kang and Kuo, 2025; Nair et al., 2023), and explicit motion prediction (Wen et al., 2024; Zheng et al.; Gao et al., 2025), aiming to capture task-relevant structure while reducing the complexity of pixel-space modeling. An outstanding line of work is the JEPA family (Assran et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026a; Maes et al., 2026; Assran et al., 2025; Balestriero and LeCun, 2025), which jointly learns to encode observations into compact latent space and models transition dynamics by predicting future latents. While JEPA provides compelling paradigm for latent world modeling, these methods can suffer from representation collapse, where the latent space degenerates toward trivial solutions, thus requiring carefully designed training strategies and regularization at the expense of expressivity loss (Wang et al., 2026a; Maes et al., 2026). Both the aforementioned video world models and latent world models are exclusively constructed in discrete-time, which potentially become inefficient when capturing the fundamental higher-order physics in reality (Cellier and Greifeneder, 2013; Krishnapriyan et al., 2023). In contrast, our proposed ODEWorld is directly modeled in continuous time while avoiding the representation collapse issue in JEPA frameworks by design, thereby offering great efficiency to model the physical world. ODE dynamics modeling. Modeling continuous dynamical systems through ordinary differential equations has found extensive applications across diverse scientific domains, including physics (Anderson and Wendt, 1995; Grigorenko and Grigorenko, 2003; Brunton et al., 2016), climate science (Trenberth and Trenberth, 1992), and neuroscience (Izhikevich, 2007). One prominent methodology involves explicitly constructing physics-informed learnable ODE dynamics (Brunton et al., 2016; Champion et al., 2019; Greydanus et al., 2019). While these methods effectively embed known invariant properties into the network structure, they strictly require explicit prior knowledge of the true underlying governing equations or given set of analytical terms to model the system dynamics, thereby severely limiting their expressiveness. Within this data-driven paradigm, classic approaches like Koopman operator theory (Mezić, 2005) are frequently employed in the control community. However, it also suffers from computationally expensive coordinate transformations and remains fundamentally restricted to an approximation of the true system dynamics. To circumvent the reliance on prior knowledge, neural ODE networks that learn neural ODE dynamic models directly from observation data have received increasing interest (Chen et al., 2018; Dupont et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Huh et al., 2020). Despite being promising, training such neural ODE networks often relies on computationally expensive adjoint method (Chen et al., 2018), which is hard to scale and often suffers from instability during training. By contrast, in our proposed PT-Flow paradigm, we directly supervise the latent ODE velocity field with the approximated ground truth latent velocities, which reconciles the preservation of ODE properties with efficient and scalable training.

sections.title: 3 Physical-Time Flow
sections.content: To transcend the discrete-time modeling to new architecture capturing continuous-time physical reality, we introduce the concept of Physical-Time Flow (PT-Flow). The core idea of PT-Flow is to capture the underlying dynamics of high-dimensional data as continuous velocity field within proper latent space. Let st Rds denote the state input at physical time t, and zt Rdz be properly encoded latent representation of st. Here, represents the physical time elapsed after starting at the initial state s0. In our setting, s0 can be flexibly selected from any frame in demonstration rather than only the first frame. Accordingly, is defined as the relative temporal offset between s0 and st. To capture the time-evolving dynamics of the physical system, straightforward approach is to learn time-dependent velocity field defined via the ordinary differential equation: dzt dt = vθ(zt, t; z0, c) = zT = z0 + (cid:90) 0 vθ(zt, t; z0, c)dt (1) where z0 is the latent representation of the initial state s0 and is the target conditioning (e.g., goal state or language instruction), that jointly specify the start and end state of the system. If we can learn such latent velocity field vθ, then future prediction can be redefined as temporal integration task over 3 the continuous physical time, thereby unlocking many interesting capabilities, such as arbitrary temporal resolution or backward prediction, as well as being amenable to many nice properties in control theory (Cellier and Greifeneder, 2013). The remaining questions are, what is the "proper" latent space and how can we learn vθ with discrete-time supervision data? Dynamical representation decoupling. Obviously, not all dynamical systems can be modeled as an ODE function, especially for nuanced mixtures of visual features in video. Ideally, for video data, we do not want to learn velocity field to fit every static background detail and time-invariant object, but want to extract clean, essential dynamics-related representations zt out of the state space. To achieve this, we learn pair of initial state-conditioned encoder and decoder: fdyn(st; s0) = zt and gdyn(zt; s0) = st. By explicitly isolating static context (time-invariant part between s0 and st) in both encoder and decoder, we make the encoded latent representation zt focus exclusively on dynamical changes. The above equation suggests that zt can be directly obtained utilizing Jacobian-vector product (JVP) projection, i.e., zt = JVP(fdyn(st; s0), st). As st can be directly approximated from training samples, i.e., simply calculating as st = (st+1 st)/t (t is the time interval between two consecutive states) or adopting more advanced higher-order estimation tricks as we will describe in the next section, the evaluation of zt is practically feasible. This enables us to introduce the following learning objective for the latent velocity field vθ, which directly supervises it with the approximated ground-truth latent velocities zt: Lv = Es0,stD,tvθ(zt, t; z0, c) sg(JVP(fdyn(st; s0), st))2, (4) We use the stop-gradient operation sg() to stabilize the optimization of the latent velocity field, following common practices in representation learning (Chen and He, 2021). Interestingly, we find that PT-Flow remains effective even without stop-gradient, as shown in App. B.6. This suggests that the proposed objective itself can provide effective constraints for learning meaningful representations. Unlike existing JEPA-style latent world models (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025) that supervise the latent predictor via the consistency loss between current and predicted embeddings, PT-FLow employs direct first-order supervision strategy to specifically optimize the latent velocity field, effectively decoupling the dynamics learning from embedding reconstruction. Such design greatly mitigates the risk of representation collapse (Wang et al., 2026a; Maes et al., 2026) in JEPA frameworks, and ensures the latent manifold remains expressive and dynamically meaningful. By jointly optimizing the loss objectives Ldyn-recon and Lv, we can learn well-structured latent space and velocity field, in which the future prediction at an arbitrary time can be achieved by integrating with an off-the-shelf ODE solver in the compact latent space.

sections.title: 4 ODEWorld: Latent World Modeling via PT-Flow
sections.content: In this section, we instantiate the PT-Flow paradigm as ODEWorld (illustrated in Fig. 1(c)), highly versatile and efficient continuous-time predictive architecture for both high-fidelity video generation and effective robotic policy learning. 4 Figure 1 Illustration of PT-Flow and ODEWorld. (a), (b) Comparison between flow matching and our proposed PT-Flow. Although both methods learn time-dependent velocity fields and perform generation with ODE solvers, their notion of time and design philosophies are completely different. (c) Model architecture of ODEWorld. Architecture overview. Apart from building PT-Flow, we first employ frozen, pre-trained DINOv2 encoder (Oquab et al., 2024) as our vision backbone fobs to project high-dimensional raw image observations xt into compressed feature space st. This transformed state space offers superior numerical stability compared to raw pixels when estimating the velocity target st in Eq. (3). Correspondingly, we train dedicated image decoder gobs to reconstruct the DINO feature back to image space ˆxt for video generation. We follow the same recipe with RAE (Zheng et al., 2026a) to train gobs with combination of L1, LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018a) and adversarial losses (Goodfellow et al., 2014): st = fobs(xt), ˆx = gobs(st), xt LDINO-recon(xt) = L1(ˆxt, xt) + ωLLLPIPS(ˆxt, xt) + ωGλLGAN(ˆxt, xt). (5) We further embed PT-Flow within the DINO feature space, where DINO image encoder and decoder fobs and gobs are frozen during the training of PT-Flow. We find that PT-Flow is sufficiently expressive to maintain consistency in latent planning and reconstruction within the DINO feature space, ultimately enabling high-fidelity video generation through gobs. Following the design of PT-Flow, we introduce an initial state-conditioned dynamics encoder fdyn and decoder gdyn, both of which are implemented using cross-attention blocks. The dynamics encoder fdyn(st; s0) = zt extracts the dynamical representation zt from the current state st conditioned on the initial state s0, where few learnable query tokens attend to both st and s0 as keys and values, producing compact latent representation that summarizes temporal changes between the initial and current states. The decoder gdyn shares similar structure, again with the initial state s0 injected but serves as the query, while the latent representation zt acts as keys and values. This design forces the model to reconstruct st by combining static context from s0 with dynamical information encoded in zt, thereby preventing zt from carrying static content. In our experiments, we find that single token is sufficient to model zt while achieving strong performance. Specifically, zt R1768 is highly compact compared to st R1616768 in original DINO space. More importantly, this result further supports the key insight of latent world modeling (Assran et al., 2023; Maes et al., 2026): raw pixels contain substantial redundancy, while the underlying dynamics can be effectively captured by much smaller latent representation. Based on the compact zt, we parameterize the velocity network vθ(zt, t; z0, c) by lightweight 3-layer MLP. The time is incorporated by Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) layers (Perez et al., 2018), while other parts are concatenated and fed into the model as input. Such compact latent dynamics model design makes the latent planning and prediction with the ODE solver extremely efficient, while maximally preserving information for image reconstruction. 5 Additional enhancements on PT-Flow. To ensure numerical stability, instead of modeling the latent velocity vθ(zt, t; z0, c) with the actual physical time as in Eq. (1), we implement vθ(zt, τ ; z0, c) based on rescaled physical time τ , where τ = and is normalizing horizon length which is approximately the desired planning length. This will make sure τ mostly resides within the range [0, 1] during training. Under this reparameterization, sτ corresponds to st scaled by in time dimension. We assume that the system reaches stationary state once the target condition is reached (e.g., the goal state zg or language instruction lg). Therefore, when τ exceeds the rescaled time index τc of the last frame in training sequence ending with condition c, we fix the future state sτ >τc to the last frame and drive the velocity field vθ to zero. To enhance the estimation quality of the target velocity st for JVP projection in Eq. (4), we employ SavitzkyGolay derivative filter (Saramäki et al., 1993), which performs local polynomial regression over sliding window. Specifically, given sequence of states {stk, . . . , st+k} within window of size 2k + 1, the target velocity is calculated as linear convolution: i=k wist+i, where wi are fixed coefficients obtained by fitting low-order polynomial in least-squares sense. In our implementation, we instantiate this filter with window size of 2k + 1 = 5, yielding filter kernel = 1 10 [2, 1, 0, 1, 2]. Unlike conventional smoothing kernels that blindly average signals (e.g., Gaussian blurring) or standard finite difference kernels, the chosen SavitzkyGolay kernel provides decent compromise between numerical accuracy and temporal smoothness, due to its adoption of local least-squares polynomial fit. This ensures that the projected target zt (via Eq. (3)) is both temporally smooth and physically accurate, which substantially enhances the learning performance of the latent velocity field vθ. st = (cid:80)k Training and inference pipeline. With the pre-trained frozen DINO encoder fdyn and decoder gdyn, the training of ODEWorld strictly follows the recipe of PT-Flow described in Section 3, which jointly minimizes the dynamics reconstruction loss Ldyn-recon (Eq. 5) and the velocity supervision loss Lv (Eq. 4), i.e., = λrecLdyn-recon + λvLv (6) In our experiments, we find that simply setting the weighting parameters λrec = λv = 1 without any tuning generally leads to reasonably good results. This further demonstrated the learning robustness of our proposed PT-Flow framework. During inference, ODEWorld serves as continuous-time ODE engine for both high-fidelity video synthesis and efficient latent planning. The inference pipeline works as follows: given an initial raw observation x0 and target condition c, the model first projects the observation into the DINO space s0 = fobs(x0) and then encodes this state into the dynamical latent space z0 = fdyn(s0; s0). We can employ any off-the-shelf ODE solver, i.e. fourth-order Runge-Kutta method (RK4), to integrate the learned velocity field vθ by zτ = z0 + (cid:82) τ 0 vθ(zt, t; z0, c)dt to predict the latent state zτ at arbitrary time τ [0, 1]. The evolved latent state zτ can then be used for: 1) future video frame generation: the latent state is sequentially mapped back to the pixel space with ˆsτ = gdyn(zτ ; s0) and ˆxτ = gobs(ˆsτ ); and 2) downstream policy learning: zτ serves as compact, dynamically meaningful subgoal. Its low-dimensional dynamics-centric nature provides stable target for policy learning, bypassing the complexity of high-dimensional visual planning. notable advantage of ODEWorld lies in its remarkable inference speed. By operating within the compact latent manifold and utilizing shallow MLP to parameterize the velocity field vθ, the numerical integration becomes computationally lightweight. This efficiency allows for real-time video generation and fast iterative latent planning, facilitating responsive closed-loop control in complex environments.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setups
sections.content: Datasets. We train ODEWorld on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) simulation dataset and AgiBot-World (Bu et al., 2025) real-world robot datasets. LIBERO consists of 130 tasks with 6,500 high-quality human teleoperation demonstrations, covering diverse motions and atomic skills. We use the full dataset to train ODEWorld and all baseline models for image generation. For the AgiBot-World, We train ODEWorld on the AgiBotWorldChallenge-2025 subset, large-scale embodied manipulation benchmark built upon the AgiBot World Colosseo platform (Bu et al., 2025). The dataset contains approximately 30K manipulation 6 Figure 2 Data trajectories in different latent spaces. ODEWorld produces significantly smoother trajectories in its dynamical latent space across various LIBERO tasks compared to the latent spaces of DINO and the next-step prediction baseline. trajectories with an average length of around 260 frames per trajectory, providing diverse robot-object interaction behaviors with visual observations across various real-world manipulation tasks. More details about datasets are provided in App. A.1. Baselines. To evaluate the video generation quality of ODEWorld, we compare it against latent world models that also support reconstruction from semantic representations. Specifically, we consider Latent Diffusion Planning (LDP) (Xie et al., 2025) and V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025). LDP employs reconstruction-based VAE latent space and performs planning and policy learning within this latent space, with generated latents decoded back into images via VAE decoder. V-JEPA 2 jointly learns representation encoder and latent predictor, and similarly decodes predicted latents into raw images through learned decoder. These models serve as suitable baselines for assessing generative quality in latent world model settings. As for policy learning, we compare ODEWorld against planning-based baselines, including the editing-based subgoal planner SuSIE (Black et al., 2024) and the end-to-end predictive inverse dynamics model Seer (Tian et al., 2025), the video prediction policy (Hu et al., 2025), and vanilla goal-and-language-conditioned behavior cloning (GLCBC) policy. More details about these baselines are provided in App. A.3 and App. A.4.

sections.title: 5.2 Visualization
sections.content: Latent space analysis. In Fig. 2, we compare the latent space of ODEWorld against the raw DINO feature space and the latent of discrete next-step predictive baseline. For the latter, we replace vθ with discrete transition model zt+1 = pθ(zt; c), remove dynamical representation decoupling designs in fdyn and gdyn, and then optimize pθ with JEPA-style objectives (Assran et al., 2023). PCA visualizations for latent trajectories from multiple LIBERO tasks reveal that ODEWorld yields the smoothest latent trajectories. This is attributed to our direct first-order supervision, which regularizes the manifold by aligning it with an analytically filtered velocity target that effectively suppresses high-frequency jitters. Crucially, while ODEWorld enhances dynamical smoothness, it maintains manifold topology remarkably similar to the original DINO space. Unlike over-regularized models that tend to straighten the latent space to achieve smoothness at the expense of expressivity, ODEWorld latent preserves the principal components and the relative geometric structure in the original space. This structural fidelity ensures that the learned latent space retains rich semantic information, providing high-fidelity foundation for downstream tasks such as video generation and subgoal planning for policy learning. Velocity field and open-loop latent planning. In the middle row of Fig. 3, we sample uniform grid in the projected PCA space and utilize the learned velocity field vθ to compute the instantaneous latent velocities at each point. These are visualized as vector field with arrows, the color of which represents the magnitude of dynamical transition. Starting from latent state at random time of the sampled trajectory, we perform long-horizon rollout using an ODE solver (RK4) to integrate the velocity vθ along normalized 7 Figure 3 Velocity field and latent planning. Middle are visualization of globally consistent goal-directed convergence of velocity field and smooth latent plans from ODEWorld that adhere well to the ground truth. The top are ground truth frames, and the bottom are synthesized frames. Figure 4 The continuous formulation enables ODEWorld to perform both forward and backward prediction, with motion consistent with real-world dynamics. We present the results on LIBERO benchmark and Agibot World. More results are provided in the Appendix. time τ without any further environmental observations. To verify semantic fidelity, the integrated latent trajectory zτ is passed through the decoders to synthesize image-space predictions shown in the bottom row, which are then compared against the ground-truth video sequence shown in the top row. The visualization reveals three key properties: (1) The velocity field captures the time-varying magnitude of the dynamics: in this example, the robot first approaches the handle and then pulls the drawer out, and the velocity correctly decays toward zero as the robot reaches the handle before accelerating again into the pulling phase. This shows that the learned velocity field encodes not only the direction toward the goal, but also the correct instantaneous speed at each stage of the task. (2) The model demonstrates high physical consistency even during open-loop planning. The planned trajectory (red line) adheres closely to the ground-truth latent path (gray line), while effectively filtering out the high-frequency noise and jitter present in the latter. (3) Finally, the synthesized predictions in the bottom row remain spatially coherent and semantically accurate. This combination of planning accuracy and smoothness provides stable, jerk-free foundation for downstream high-fidelity video generation and precise subgoal planning for policy learning. 8 Figure 5 ODEWorld allows any resolution generation with flexible temporal speed. Based on this, ODEWorld can generalize beyond the sampling rate of the training data. In particular, when trained on temporally downsampled sequences, the model is able to generate smooth and coherent intermediate frames, performing temporal super-resolution and filling in missing observations.

sections.title: 5.3 ODEWorld for Video Generation
sections.content: Bidirectional video generation. As demonstrated in Fig. 4, ODEWorld exhibits unique bidirectional flexibility inherent to its ODE-governed architecture. By simply reversing the integration sign (vτ vτ ), the model can synthesize physically plausible backward video sequences from the same learned latent velocity field. This symmetry validates that ODEWorld internalizes the underlying continuous physics , rather than merely memorizing forward predictive patterns typical of those discrete predictive architectures. Any-resolution video generation. As illustrated in Fig. 5, ODEWorld leverages its continuous, ODE-governed nature to achieve arbitrary temporal resolution in video generation. Unlike discrete models constrained by fixed step sizes, our model can generate motion at any speed (Fig. 5(a)) and effectively interpolate missing frames (Fig. 5(b)). sections.title: 5.4 ODEWorld for Policy Learning
sections.content: We assess how ODEWorld can empower downstream policy learning by inferring latent subgoals as guidance. We instantiate three guidance paradigms: (1) velocity-conditioned π(az, c, v), (2) single-subgoal π(az, c, ˆzτ ), τ = 0.25, and (3) sequential-subgoal π(az, c, {ˆzτi}n i=1), = 5, τi = 0.05i, where subgoals are generated via ODE integration. denotes image goal and language instruction. Results on LIBERO-LONG. As shown in Tab. 2, all ODEWorld variants outperform the baselines on LIBERO-LONG. Among them, the sequential-subgoal paradigm achieves the best performance with an average success rate of 83.2%. This performance gain demonstrates the high-fidelity temporal consistency of ODEWorld rollouts; by maintaining precise trajectory alignment over horizon, the model provides dense and reliable guidance that does not drift from the task objective. Such consistent sequential subgoal guidance effectively benefits downstream policy learning. Results on real-world robot experiments. To further validate the effectiveness of ODEWorld beyond simulation benchmarks, we conduct real-world control experiments on bi-manual AgileX robot. We use X-VLA (Zheng et al., 2026b) as the policy backbone and augment it with ODEWorld-generated latent subgoals for guidance. We evaluate four manipulation tasks, including: Shrimp-to-pot, Mouse packing, Pen insertion, 10 Bi-manual rearrangement. Detailed task settings are provided in App. A.2. Using the same policy backbone and training protocol, ODEWorld improves the average success rate from 55% to 80% across these four tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of ODEWorld-generated dynamics guidance in real-world manipulation scenarios.

sections.title: 6 Conclusions
sections.content: We introduce ODEWorld, novel continuous latent world model grounded in physical time. The core of ODEWorld is new predictive paradigm called PT-Flow, which learns latent ODE velocity field defined on physical time. It recasts future prediction as temporal integration with the latent velocity via an ODE solver, which shares some similarities to flow matching, but operates in physical time rather than the noise space. Through comprehensive experiments on both simulation and real-world benchmark datasets, we show that ODEWorld enjoys number of desirable properties, such as interpretable latent velocity fields, prediction with arbitrary direction or temporal resolutions, high-quality reconstruction after long-term prediction, and facilitative planning-centric representation for downstream policy learning. Many of the above properties are fundamentally absent in most discrete-time predictive models. We anticipate that PT-Flow and ODEWorld will inspire new generation of predictive models, paving the way for more faithful understanding and modeling of the continuous physical world.

sections.title: A Experiment Details
sections.content: A.1 Datasets LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023). LIBERO is large-scale language-conditioned robotic manipulation benchmark comprising 130 tasks and 6,500 high-quality human teleoperation demonstrations. These tasks span diverse set of atomic and compositional skills, including grasping, lifting, placing, opening, and multi-step object rearrangement. The benchmark is organized into five suites, namely LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, LIBERO-90, and LIBERO-Long, each targeting distinct generalization capabilities such as spatial reasoning, object-level variation, goal specification, and long-horizon compositional manipulation. Following the standard evaluation protocol, we use the official LIBERO dataset and re-render all observations at resolution of 256 256 to ensure controlled comparison across methods. We train ODEWorld and all image-generation baselines on the full dataset. AgiBot-World (Bu et al., 2025). For AgiBot-World, we train ODEWorld on the AgiBotWorldChallenge-2025 subset, large-scale embodied manipulation benchmark built on the AgiBot World Colosseo platform (Bu et al., 2025). The subset used in our experiments contains approximately 30K manipulation trajectories, with an average length of around 260 frames per trajectory. It captures diverse robot-object interaction patterns and provides visual observations across wide range of real-world manipulation tasks. Compared with existing short-horizon robot datasets, its relatively long trajectories and rich interaction dynamics make it well suited for continuous-time world modeling and future visual prediction. LIBERO-LONG. As subset of LIBERO, LIBERO-LONG focuses on long-horizon compositional manipulation, where each episode requires completing multiple sequential subgoals involving interactions with several objects. The benchmark consists of ten tasks: (1) Soup and sauce to basket, (2) Box and butter to basket, (3) Turn on the stove and place the pot, (4) Bowl to drawer, (5) Mugs on plates, (6) Book to rack, (7) Mug and pudding, (8) Soup and box to basket, (9) Both pots on the stove, and (10) Mug to microwave. A.2 Real-World Settings We follow recent SOTA practice (Black et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Feng et al.) to conduct real-world robotics experiments on bi-manual AgileX robot equipped with two 6-DoF robotic arms, parallel-jaw grippers, and RGB cameras. We use X-VLA (Zheng et al., 2026b) as the policy backbone and incorporate ODEWorld-generated latent subgoals for sequential guidance. All experiments are conducted under the same training and evaluation protocol for fair comparison with the original X-VLA policy. We evaluate ODEWorld on four manipulation tasks: (1) Shrimp-to-pot: Place shrimp into pot; (2) Mouse packing: Pack mouse into box; (3) Pen insertion: Grasp thin pen and insert it into narrow container, requiring fine-grained perception and precise control; (4) Bi-manual rearrangement: Simultaneously move objects using both arms in complex scene, evaluating coordinated bi-manual control and multi-object dynamics modeling. Fig. 6 presents the initial states of these four real-world manipulation tasks. Figure 6 Initial states of the four real-world manipulation tasks. From left to right: Shrimp-to-pot, Mouse packing, Pen insertion, and Bi-manual rearrangement. 16 A.3 Video Genertaion Baselines V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025). We adopt the pre-trained V-JEPA 2 ViT-L/16 checkpoint as the visual representation backbone and fine-tune it on LIBERO demonstration videos from the agentview camera. The model follows the standard online-target encoder design of V-JEPA 2, where the target encoder is updated by EMA. During training, we use short video clips cropped to 256 256 and apply first-tubelet-visible masking strategy, forcing the predictor to infer future latent tokens from the initial visible spatio-temporal context. To incorporate task information, we extract language features with frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 text encoder (Radford et al., 2021) and inject them into the predictor through zero-initialized cross-attention layers. Since V-JEPA 2 predicts latent representations rather than pixels, we additionally train lightweight convolutional decoder for RGB reconstruction. The encoder-predictor stack is frozen when training this decoder. To improve robustness to errors in predicted latents, we perturb the training latents with Gaussian noise. The decoder is optimized with an L1 reconstruction loss over video frames and an LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018b) loss on temporally subsampled frames. LDP (Xie et al., 2025). We implement LDP based on the official codebase and make several modifications for fair comparison under high-resolution LIBERO video modeling. Specifically, we increase the visual input resolution to 256 256 and enlarge the visual token budget in the planner/IDM pipeline accordingly. To handle the high-dimensional SD-VAE latent representation, we introduce spatial convolutional projection before policy learning, which compresses the latent feature map and stabilizes training. We also add explicit goal-image conditioning by encoding the goal frame with the same VAE and injecting the goal latent into the planning module. During inference, LDP performs open-loop rollout, where future latent trajectories are autoregressively predicted without intermediate environment feedback. These settings are used consistently for all reported LDP results. A.4 Policy Learning Baselines GLCBC. GLCBC is goal-conditioned language behavioral cloning baseline implemented within the LBP policy architecture but without the high-level planner. The current image observation is encoded by ResNet-34 (He et al., 2016), while the language instruction is encoded by CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). In addition, we use predefined final goal image as goal conditioning and encode it with the DecisionNCE image encoder (Li et al., 2024b). The language and goal-image embeddings are concatenated and injected into the policy through FiLM (Perez et al., 2018) module to modulate the visual features. Finally, the low-level diffusion policy takes the conditioned visual semantics and current proprioception as inputs, and predicts the diffusion noise for action generation. For simulation experiments, we fine-tune the released SuSIE checkpoint on the LIBERO dataset. Seer (Tian et al., 2025). We use Seer as vision-language-action baseline following its original implementation. The model predicts future visual representations from the current observation and language instruction, and then uses an inverse-dynamics head to predict actions conditioned on both the current observation and the predicted future features. VPP (Hu et al., 2025). VPP learns implicit inverse dynamics model conditioned on predicted future representations inside VDMs. To predict more precise future, VPP fine-tunes the pre-trained video foundation model on robot datasets along with internet human manipulation data. sections.title: B Ablation Studies
sections.content: B.1 Ablation on Dynamical Representation Decoupling To validate the effectiveness of our architectural design, we evaluate the impact of the dynamical representation decoupling module in ODEWorld. We observe that without explicitly isolating the static context s0 from the state space, the learned latent trajectories become significantly non-smooth and jittery as shown in Fig. 7. The primary reason is that not all nuanced visual features in raw video observation can be seamlessly modeled as an ODE function. Raw feature spaces inherently contain substantial amount of noisy, time-invariant, and non-ODE-compatible information, such as static backgrounds and object textures. Forcing continuous velocity field to fit these static details fundamentally disrupts the dynamics learning process. As shown in Tab. 4, the proposed decoupling strategy not only significantly improves inference efficiency (significantly higher FPS) but also enhances perceptual consistency (much lower LPIPS scores, especially for long-horizon prediction). We note that the non-decoupled variant attains marginally higher PSNR, which is expected rather than contradictory: as an MSE-based pixel-level metric, PSNR is dominated by large static regions (e.g., backgrounds and textures) that this variant retains and reconstructs faithfully, whereas its worse LPIPS reflects the temporal and semantic inconsistency that such per-frame fidelity does not capture. Consequently, without decoupling, the latent structure fails to effectively scaffold the direct first-order supervision to optimize the velocity field. By introducing the initial state-conditioned encoder and decoder, our decoupling mechanism ensures that the latent representation focuses exclusively on essential dynamical changes, which is crucial for learning well-behaved, temporally smooth, and physically meaningful latent flow. First, the consistency loss couples two distinct objectives prediction and reconstruction forcing the model to learn latent space that is simultaneously reconstructable and ODE-plannable. Second, this coupling is especially harmful in our setting: unlike standard dynamical systems where the goal is to fit one specific governing ODE, ODEWorld only needs to fit some admissible ODE in the latent space, so the target is underdetermined and the entangled objective adds too strict constraints to settle on consistent solution. In contrast, ODEWorld decouples these objectives via reconstruction loss and direct first-order supervision loss, optimizing each independently, which leads to more stable optimization and, in turn, better video generation quality. B.3 Ablations on Vision Encoders We examine how ODEWorld is compatible with different choices of vision feature extractors by replacing DINOv2 with SigLIP 2 (Tschannen et al., 2025) and LIV (Ma et al., 2023). As shown in Tab. 5, ODEWorld maintains robust video generation quality across all three encoders. While the gaps are small, DINOv2 achieves the best overall performance on both shortand long-horizon prediction, consistent with its widely recognized effectiveness as visual encoder. B.4 Ablation on Token Numbers We increase the number of token from 1 to 4 and keep other configurations unchanged. Results in Tab. 6 show comparable performance between 1and 4-token models, indicating that single latent token is already sufficient to achieve strong performance across the evaluated scenarios. This also indicates that our key designs make ODEWorld capable of efficiently capturing the underlying dynamics from pixels with very compact latent representation. B.5 ODEWorld with Different Goal Descriptions ODEWorld naturally supports image goals, where the target image provides explicit visual guidance for future dynamics prediction. However, in practical scenarios, goals are often specified by language instructions. To extend ODEWorld to language-based goal descriptions, we introduce lightweight goal image predictor to bridge the language and visual modalities. Specifically, since ODEWorld adopts DINOv2 as the visual backbone rather than large-scale vision-language model, we avoid introducing additional multimodal alignment complexity into the dynamics model. Instead, we train lightweight goal image predictor consisting of four cross-attention layers, which takes the current observation and language instruction as inputs and predicts the corresponding goal image. As shown in Fig. 8, the goal image predictor generates semantically meaningful goal images from the current observation and language instruction, providing effective visual guidance for ODEWorld. 19 Figure 8 Qualitative results of the goal image predictor. sections.title: E Limitations
sections.content: Although our proposed framework provides promising architecture for continuous-time predictive modeling, the current version of ODEWorld still has several limitations and can be further enhanced in future research. First, while the proposed ODEWorld demonstrates some impressive capabilities and efficiency, its scale and amount of training data (two robotics datasets) remain small as compared to many large video-based world models. This limitation stems primarily from computational resource constraints. Future studies can be conducted to further scale the model size and train on larger and more diverse datasets. Second, our current version of ODEWorld uses frozen DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) image encoder to encode raw observations. As DINO is designed to encode single-frame images without much consideration for temporal consistency, it could produce noisy and temporally inconsistent embeddings for sequential modeling. In our study, we introduce the SavitzkyGolay derivative filter (Saramäki et al., 1993) to enhance the smoothness and approximation quality of the ground truth velocity target to mitigate the deficiencies of the DINO encoder. Further investigations can consider replacing DINO with an image encoder with temporal consistency design (Li et al., 2024b) or jointly tuning the DINO encoder during model training. Lastly, current version of ODEWorld does not incorporate action conditioning and primarily focuses on video generation. Future studies can consider injecting action conditioning into pre-trained ODEWorld model, which can further unlock its capability for control tasks.
